title: Bus Routes
description: Brute force to optimized: plain BFS over stop transitions (incorrect) versus BFS over buses, riding entire routes at once.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a list of bus routes (each route is a list of stops that a bus cycles through repeatedly), a source stop, and a target stop, return the minimum number of BUSES needed to travel from source to target, or -1 if impossible.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","routes, source, target"],["Output","Fewest buses needed, or -1"],["Key Insight","BFS should treat a BUS RIDE (reaching every stop on that bus's route at once) as one \"step\", not an individual stop"],["Constraints","Up to 500 routes"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Minimum number of a coarse-grained UNIT (buses), not individual small steps (stops)\"","BFS where the natural \"step\" unit is boarding an entire bus (reaching all its stops simultaneously), not moving between adjacent stops one at a time"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

The key realization is that boarding a SINGLE bus grants access to EVERY stop on that bus's entire route in one "step" (one bus ride), regardless of how many stops that involves. So BFS should operate over BUSES as the unit of movement: from the current set of reachable stops, find every UNVISITED bus passing through any of them, "ride" each such bus (marking every stop on its route as newly reachable), and this constitutes one level of BFS, corresponding to one additional bus ridden.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Transfers on a Transit System, Not Individual Stops Passed
blocks.text: Picture counting the fewest transit LINES you need to ride to get from one station to another, where boarding any single line gives you access to every station on that line's entire route in one "hop" (one boarding). This is fundamentally different from counting individual stations passed, since one bus ride can span many stations at once.

blocks.caption: Map each stop to every bus passing through it; boarding a bus reaches ALL its stops in ONE step

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: routes=[[1,2,7],[3,6,7]], source=1, target=6
Result: 2 (board bus 0 from stop 1 reaching stop 7, then bus 1 from stop 7 reaching stop 6).
Result: -1 (no combination of buses connects stop 15 to stop 12).
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If source equals target, 0 buses are needed.

Observation 2: Precompute a map from every stop to the list of bus indices passing through it, since this is needed repeatedly during the search.

Observation 3: Run BFS where each LEVEL represents riding one additional bus: starting from the source stop, find every bus (not yet ridden) passing through any currently reachable stop, and "ride" each one, marking EVERY stop on its route as newly reachable (all in the SAME level, since boarding one bus reaches all its stops in a single step).

Observation 4: If the target stop is ever found among a newly reached bus's stops, the CURRENT level (number of buses ridden so far, including this one) is the answer; if the search exhausts all buses without ever reaching the target, return -1.
This leads to BFS over buses (not individual stops), where riding one bus reaches all of its stops simultaneously in a single level.
6. Brute Force Solution
Conceptually, run a BFS treating each individual adjacent stop transition as one step, without recognizing that an entire bus route should count as just one step.
Why the code is written this way

items: Connecting stops on the same route and running plain BFS seems like a natural graph modeling of the problem.
This fundamentally miscounts the answer, since it treats each stop transition as a separate step, when riding a whole bus route (reaching all its stops) should count as exactly ONE step (one bus).

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total stops squared) potentially, and produces an INCORRECT answer besides.
Space: O(total stops) for the stop graph.
Limitation: BFS must operate over BUSES as the unit of movement, not individual stops, to correctly count the minimum number of bus rides.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: If source equals target, return 0 immediately. Build a map from every stop to the list of bus indices passing through it. Run BFS: seed the queue with the source stop, track visited buses and visited stops. At each level (representing one additional bus ridden), for every stop in the current queue, find every UNVISITED bus passing through it; for each such bus, mark it visited, and for every stop on that bus's ENTIRE route, if it is the target, return the current bus count; otherwise, if unvisited, mark it visited and add it to the next level's queue. Increment the bus count after each level. If the queue empties without finding the target, return -1.
Use BFS over buses: each level represents riding one additional bus, reaching all its stops simultaneously.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for routes=[[1,2,7],[3,6,7]], source=1, target=6

blocks.content: {"headers":["BFS level (buses ridden)","Action"],"rows":[["1","from stop 1, ride bus 0, reaching stops 1,2,7"],["2","from stop 7, ride bus 1, reaching stops 3,6,7; stop 6 is the TARGET, return 2"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since boarding any bus grants immediate access to EVERY stop on its route in a single "ride", treating each BFS level as "one more bus ridden" (rather than "one more stop reached") correctly matches the true cost structure of the problem; marking buses (not just stops) as visited prevents wastefully re-riding the same bus, and BFS's natural level-by-level guarantee ensures the target is found at the true minimum number of buses needed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total stops across all routes), each stop and bus processed a bounded number of times.
Space: O(total stops) for the stop-to-buses map and visited sets.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Bus Routes teaches a subtle but crucial BFS lesson: correctly identifying the true "unit of movement" (a bus ride, not a stop) is essential, since counting the wrong unit produces a genuinely incorrect answer, not just a slower one.
Common Mistakes

items: Modeling the graph as stop-to-stop connections and running plain BFS, which fundamentally miscounts the number of buses (a genuine correctness bug, not just inefficiency).
Forgetting to mark BUSES visited (only marking stops), potentially re-riding the same bus repeatedly and never terminating correctly.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["source equals target","Returns 0 immediately, no bus needed."],["No sequence of buses connects source to target","Returns -1."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "the BFS level represents one bus ridden, not one stop reached" heads off the single most common and serious bug in this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimum transfers on a transit system, boarding a line grants access to its ENTIRE route at once", think: BFS where each level represents boarding one additional line, not moving one stop.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also reconstruct the actual sequence of buses to board, not just the count?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Word Ladder, another BFS problem where the "unit of movement" (a full letter substitution generating many candidates) must be correctly identified.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Plain BFS over stop transitions is not just slower, it is INCORRECT; BFS over buses costs O(total stops), the standard correct and efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: BFS where the unit of movement is a coarse-grained "bus ride", not an individual stop.
Core Idea: boarding a bus reaches every stop on its route simultaneously, in one BFS level.
Time: plain stop-based BFS is both slower and incorrect; the bus-based BFS costs O(total stops).
Space: O(total stops) for the bus-based approach.
Most Important Observation: counting buses (not stops) is a correctness requirement, not merely an efficiency choice.
Interview Difficulty: a hard, subtly tricky BFS problem.
One line memory trick: BFS over buses; riding one reaches its whole route at once.
